name: Gane
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The wordlists are written in the official spelling of the Indonesian language. The sounds are more or less identical with those of Indonesian. [...] Geminate consonants as in dilla, daddoba are to be pronounced twice as long as a single consonant. Stress is indicated by the symbol ´, as in kiklé, pobóilo, if the word does not stress the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Teljeur, Dirk. 1982. Short wordlists from South Halmahera, Kayoa, Makian, Ternate, Tidore and Bacan. In C. L. Voorhoeve (ed.), The Makian languages and their neighbours (Pacific Linguistics D-46), 129-148. Canberra: Department of Linguistics, RSPacS, Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: p. 132 (PDF page 140), introductory note to the wordlists; Gane rows pp. 133-148 (e.g. p. 133 items 1-9, p. 143 items 75-82)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: opened (156 pp., sealang CC BY-SA edition of PL D-46; chapter DOI 10.15144/PL-D46.129) at printed p. 132 = PDF page 140 and the saved page image. The passage is there verbatim: "The wordlists are written in the official spelling of the Indonesian language. The sounds are more or less identical with those of Indonesian. [...] Geminate consonants as in dilla, daddoba are to be pronounced twice as long as a single consonant. Stress is indicated by the symbol ´, as in kiklé, pobóilo, if the word does not stress the penultimate syllable." The ellipsis covers the o/ei pronunciation notes only. IDENTITY: p. 131 item I.5 "Gane (Gimán), spoken in the villages of Gane Dalam (Gimán Pulilò) and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orthographic convention for the whole set of wordlists (Weda, Foya/Mafa, Wosi, Gane, Saketa, Kayoa, Makian dialects, Ternate, Tidore, Bacan, Bajo): stress is on the penultimate syllable unless an acute marks another syllable. In the Gane column the words are almost all unmarked (p. 133: kikle 'hair', tinge 'ear', mto 'eye', mimou 'tongue', koku 'neck', where the neighbouring Wosi and Saketa forms carry final-stress acutes kiklé, tingé, mtó), so Gane words are to be read with penultimate stress; the only marked Gane form seen is lóal 'big' (p. 143), an acute on the first vowel of a vowel sequence.
new_statements.exceptions: Non-penultimate stress is possible and is marked with an acute; the Gane column shows essentially none (contrast Wosi/Saketa final-stress forms).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation-form words in a 200-item comparative wordlist; not a phonological description and not Gane-specific (a convention for all the languages listed). Village-level dialects: Gane Dalam (Gimán Pulilò) and Gane Luar (Giman Pulikin), about 1500 speakers in 1982 (p. 131).
new_statements.identity_note: The 1982 wordlist covers Gane (Gimán) as spoken in Gane Dalam (Gimán Pulilò) and Gane Luar (Giman Pulikin), South Halmahera (Teljeur 1982: 131), i.e. gane1237 itself; the stress convention is stated for all languages in the wordlist set, not for Gane alone. The Burhanuddin et al. papers also treat Gane (gzn) as one of six South Halmahera Austronesian languages.

sources.note: p. 132, orthographic note for all the wordlists (incl. Gane): stress is marked with an acute only when it is not on the penultimate syllable; the Gane rows (e.g. p. 133 kikle, tinge, mto, mimou, koku) carry no marks where neighbouring Wosi/Saketa rows do (kiklé, tingé, mtó), i.e. Gane words are read as penultimate-stressed; one Gane form lóal 'big' (p. 143) carries an acute on the first vowel of a vowel sequence.
